logline: Awkward startup founder Richard Hendricks builds a world-changing compression algorithm and is immediately surrounded by everyone who wants to destroy, steal, or invest in it.

seasons.review_body: Silicon Valley's first season landed in April 2014 as one of HBO's sharpest comedy commissions in years. The 95% Rotten Tomatoes score and Metacritic 84 reflected enthusiasm for Mike Judge - who had spent Office Space and Idiocracy satirising corporate and populist mediocrity - finding new, richer territory in the specific techno-utopianism of the Bay Area. Tim Goodman at The Hollywood Reporter said it was 'HBO's best and funniest full-on comedy in years.' Matt Roush at TV Guide praised 'the deft, resonant satire.' Thomas Middleditch's physically anxious Richard Hendricks was a precise comic creation: brilliant, socially paralysed, constitutionally unable to enjoy his own success.

episode_reviews.title: Optimal Tip-to-Tip Efficiency
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The Season 1 finale resolves the TechCrunch Disrupt competition with a comedy set piece that became one of the most discussed single jokes in contemporary television - a purely mathematical solution applied to an absurd problem. The episode confirmed that Silicon Valley could execute high-concept comedy with the precision of a well-engineered algorithm.
episode_reviews.the_moment: Richard's compression algorithm breakthrough is demonstrated via a calculation that required actual mathematical consultation - the show's proof that its tech satire was built on genuine rigour.

critic_note.text: HBO finds its best and funniest full-on comedy in years with this Mike Judge creation.

bollymeter.basis: Season 2 earned 96% on Rotten Tomatoes and Metacritic 86. The expanded episode count allowed the satire to deepen while maintaining the first season's comic velocity, and T.J. Miller's Erlich Bachman crystallised as the series' defining supporting creation.

seasons.review_body: Season 2 expanded to ten episodes and the 96% Rotten Tomatoes score and Metacritic 86 confirmed the series had found its stride. The show's central argument deepened - that startup culture is a cargo cult of ambition in which disruption rhetoric masks conventional corporate power struggle. Erlich Bachman (T.J. Miller) crystallised as the series' defining supporting comic creation. The writing found ways to make the technical specifics funny to non-technical audiences while remaining rigorous enough to earn industry respect.
seasons.season_over_season: More episodes gave the show room to deepen the satire without losing pace - Season 2 is the series finding its full range.

bollymeter.basis: Season 3 earned a perfect 100% on Rotten Tomatoes and Metacritic 90, the series' peak critical scores. Pied Piper's structural reinvention - repeatedly losing and rebuilding its identity - gave the comedy a genuine dramatic engine.

pull_quotes.text: The deft, resonant satire that helped make Judge's Office Space a cult hit takes on farcical new dimension.

seasons.review_body: Season 3 is the creative apex of Silicon Valley, earning a perfect 100% on Rotten Tomatoes and Metacritic 90. The season had discovered the show's ideal structural rhythm: Richard loses everything, rebuilds from first principles, and in doing so exposes another layer of the tech industry's contradictions. The Pied Piper team's shifting power dynamics - and the show's willingness to undermine its own protagonist repeatedly - gave the comedy unusual structural ambition for the format. Matt Roush at TV Guide praised 'the deft, resonant satire that helped make Judge's Office Space a cult hit' finding 'farcical new dimension.'
seasons.season_over_season: The peak - Silicon Valley's satire is at its sharpest and most structurally confident in Season 3, with the perfect RT score as external confirmation.

bollymeter.basis: The final season scored 94% on Rotten Tomatoes and Metacritic 78. The shortened run was workable as a finale, though T.J. Miller's departure in Season 5 had permanently altered the show's comic chemistry.

seasons.review_body: Season 6 wrapped Silicon Valley in seven episodes with 94% on Rotten Tomatoes. The departure of T.J. Miller's Erlich Bachman after Season 4 had shifted the comic ecology in ways the final two seasons never fully compensated for. Metacritic 78 was below the series' peaks but above the Season 5 dip. The show had earned a coherent ending - the final episode's satirical resolution of the Pied Piper story landed as appropriately dark - even if the journey there felt abbreviated by the episode reduction.
seasons.season_over_season: A fitting if not triumphant end - the shortened run and the absence of Erlich Bachman cap the ceiling, but the satire lands its final point cleanly.
